s0.p1: Human milk is the gold standard for infant feeding. Infant formula development has moved from matching human milk in nutrition, to matching its structure, and now towards matching its flavor. Infant formula is already close to human milk in macronutrients but still differs clearly in flavor, which affects how well infants accept it and may also shape their later food preferences. Identifying the key flavor compounds of human milk, and how formula differs, is the first step towards matching its flavor.
s0.p2: This page follows one human milk sample through the whole chain: sample HM0031 (HF31 below) is one of the 50 human milk samples of Cui et al. (2026, Food Bioscience, doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2026.110162), and its volatile profile is close to the average of the 50 (ranked 2nd, 3rd and 2nd of 50 by three distance measures). Steps 1 to 8 use only this sample and published data; step 9 uses the mean data of 303 human milk samples and 20 infant formulas from Cui et al. (FC_CITE). Each step gives the question, the tool (the links open the same input), the result, the interpretation and the limitations.
s1.q: Question: Which target compounds are in the GC-MS peak table of one human milk sample, and in what proportions?
s1.tool: Tool: GC-MS flavor interpreter, example 4 (the original instrument report of HF31, an Agilent MassHunter library search with 345 peak records). The standard file holds the 75 compounds and retention times of Table S1 of Cui et al. (2026, Food Bioscience, doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2026.110162); retention time range ± 0.3 min, relative content normalized to the targets, author group threshold values.
s1.r1: 27 target compounds were found, summing to 100%. Octanoic, hexanoic and decanoic acid and hexanal are the most abundant.
s1.i1: Interpretation: compared with the author's own processing program (same peak table): the author's program finds 29 of its 125 target compounds and normalizes over these 29; here 27 of the 75 Table S1 compounds are found (1-decanol and 3-heptenoic acid are not in Table S1) and the values are normalized over these 27, so each value is about 1.002 times the author's. On the same denominator (these 27 compounds), all 27 compounds agree, with a largest difference of 0.005 percentage points. The retention times in Table S1 are about 0.1 to 0.3 min earlier than those of this run, hence ± 0.3 min; ± 0.2 min misses 4 compounds such as nonanal and (E)-2-nonenal, and ± 0.1 min finds only 16.
s1.lim: Limitations: Relative contents are semi-quantitative (no internal standard). The tool does not re-identify peaks and relies on the library search; a wider range is more likely to add misidentified peaks (none here). 2,4-Di-tert-butylphenol, 2-ethyl-1-hexanol, 2-phenoxyethanol and isophorone are migrants from sampling containers and laboratory materials (Table S1, footnote A); they stay in the standard file and none was detected in HF31.
s2.q: Question: Which compounds contribute most to the aroma of HF31?
s2.tool: Tool: The “flavor interpretation” step of the same page: relative odor activity value (ROAV); example 4 selects the author group values automatically.
s2.fig: The ranking table in the tool (top 10): thresholds in mg/kg; odor descriptions from the flavor knowledge base or the model.
s2.alt: Screenshot of the ROAV ranking table of GC-MS example 4
s2.i1: Interpretation: 9 key flavor compounds have ROAV ≥ 1: eight aldehydes and one ketone, led by (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal (ROAV 100) and 1-hepten-3-one (83.4). Hexanal is the most abundant (13.1%) but has a higher threshold and ranks 6th. The ROAV uses odor detection thresholds in water (L.J. van Gemert 2011 compilation, author group values).
s2.lim: Limitations: ROAV shows only the relative contributions within one sample, not whether a compound can be smelled; the thresholds are for water, not for the milk matrix.
s3.m.18829-56-6: no cucumber in the top 8 (melon is 8th)
s3.m.124-13-0: fatty 3rd, no soapy in the top 8
s3.q: Question: Does the predicted odor agree with what was smelled at the GC-O sniffing port?
s3.tool: Tool: Odor prediction (a graph neural network giving probabilities for 138 odor descriptors). Each compound in the table links to its prediction.
s3.i1: Interpretation: of the 7 compounds with a GC-O description, 6 have a GC-O descriptor among the top 5 predictions, including the metallic note of 1-hepten-3-one (4th); cucumber-like for (E)-2-nonenal and soapy for octanal are not in the top 8.
s3.lim: Limitations: All 9 are common compounds in the model's training data (the odor prediction page shows this): 7 in the training split, (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal and octanal in the test split. The agreement says nothing about predictions for new molecules. The model does not distinguish cis/trans isomers: (E,Z)- and (E,E)-2,4-decadienal get the same prediction.
s4.q: Question: Is the FD ranking from GC-O sniffing (AEDA) reliable?
s4.tool: Tool: Gas-phase intensity curves (dose-response curves and gas-phase thresholds of Wakayama et al. 2019). The relative content in HF31 divided by the gas-phase threshold is set against the FD of the pooled sample of 50 human milks in Cui et al. (2026, Food Bioscience, doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2026.110162).
s4.i1: Interpretation: hexanal and octanal are high (both FD 64), nonanal and heptanal low (FD 4 and 1): the ranking agrees with the FD, which supports the accuracy of the GC-O sniffing results.
s4.lim: Limitations: Only these 4 aldehydes have intensity curves; the other key flavor compounds ((E,E)-2,4-nonadienal, 1-hepten-3-one, (E)-2-nonenal, (E)-2-octenal and others) have no curve in Wakayama et al. (2019) and cannot be checked.
s4.h: Step 4. Intensity curves checked against FD
s5.q: Question: Where could one start for the key compound 1-hepten-3-one: ingredients or similar molecules?
s5.tool: Tool: Ingredient and substitute search, mode B (similar molecules by cosine similarity of the predicted odor), and the compounds detected in human milk and its key flavor compounds in the flavor knowledge base.
s5.r1: The closest molecules to 1-hepten-3-one are (Z)-1,5-octadien-3-one (0.978) and 1-octen-3-one (0.977). 1-Octen-3-one is exactly the other FD 64, metallic key flavor compound of Cui et al. (2026). The aldehydes are all very similar to each other (nonanal and octanal 0.995): the model puts them in one fatty, citrus aldehyde group, so substituting one for another means little.
s5.r2: The database grew with the research: when this chain was first run, the knowledge base had only FlavorDB2: 1-hepten-3-one had no food source at all, “Milk Human” was linked to only 3 molecules, and none of the key flavor compounds of human milk was there. Adding FooDB did not change this (its human milk entries are nutrients such as fatty acids, amino acids and vitamins). So the author's published human milk data were added to the knowledge base (see update log 7.5): the human milk page now has the compounds detected by Cui et al. (2026) and 10 key flavor compounds.
s5.warn: No flavorings in infant formula: GB 2760-2024 Table B.1 states that flavorings may not be added to 13.01 infant and young child formulas; no flavoring at all may be added to formulas for infants aged 0 to 6 months; follow-on and young child formulas may use only vanillin, ethyl vanillin (5 mg/100 mL) and vanilla bean extract. Adding key flavor compounds directly is therefore not an option for infant formula, and improvement can only start from precursors (fatty acid composition, lipid sources); see steps 7 to 9.
s5.lim: Limitations: Mode B compares predicted odor only and does not show whether a molecule can replace another; FlavorDB2 records presence only, with no amounts.
s6.q: Question: Where do the molecules detected in human milk lie in odor space?
s6.tool: Tool: Odor map with human milk and cow milk overlaid (over 5,000 molecules arranged by predicted odor).
s6.fig: Human milk (blue; large dots: the 10 key flavor compounds) and cow milk (red) on the odor map; grey: other molecules.
s6.alt: Odor map screenshot: positions of human milk and cow milk molecules
s6.r1: The 99 molecules linked to human milk in the knowledge base lie mainly in the fatty and green regions (top predicted descriptor: fatty 22, green 20, together 42%); the 207 molecules of cow milk are more spread out (odorless 29, fruity 28, fatty 22, green 16, phenolic 12, fishy 11, sulfurous 9; fatty and green together 18%). The 10 key flavor compounds of human milk (Cui et al. 2026, Table 1) are shown as large dots. Of these 99 molecules, 78 come from Cui et al. (2026) and 29 from FooDB (10 of them from both), and 2 only from FlavorDB2; the knowledge base links 100 molecules to human milk in all, but thiamine is not in the odor map's molecule library.
s6.i1: Interpretation: consistent with human milk aroma being dominated by aldehydes and ketones from lipid oxidation.
s6.lim: Limitations: The two sources are not comparable: human milk comes from the author's published data, cow milk from FlavorDB2 and FooDB. This does not show that cow milk lacks these compounds (many bulk entries are hidden, or the public databases have not recorded them).
s7.q: Question: If improvement starts from precursors, what do the candidate additions linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid taste like themselves?
s7.tool: Tool: Taste prediction (a graph neural network for sweet, bitter, umami and tasteless; judgement thresholds sweet 58%, bitter 42%, umami 18%, chosen on the validation split).
s7.i1: Interpretation: both linoleic and α-linolenic acid are predicted bitter, above the judgement threshold. Both are in the training data (labelled bitter), so this reads as “the training data record bitter, the prediction agrees, and so does the literature”: Stephan et al. (2000) found free linoleic and linolenic acid to have the lowest bitter thresholds in emulsions and to be the main source of the bitterness of soybean lecithin; Gläser et al. (2021) found free α-linolenic and linoleic acid to be key bitter compounds in pea protein; the bitter compounds identified by Huseynli et al. (2025) in sunflower press cake include α-linolenic, linoleic, oleic, palmitic and stearic acid; Cheon et al. (2021) report that C18 free fatty acids are mainly described as bitter. Eicosanoic acid, not in the training data, is also predicted bitter (56%), in the same direction as Cheon et al. (2021); this is a single example and no proof of the model's ability.
s7.i2: In infant formula, fatty acids are added as triglycerides (oils). Mattes (2009) notes that triglycerides themselves are not effective taste stimuli, unlike free fatty acids; the model's output for triglycerides is an extrapolation and is not used here.
s7.h3: Supplement: free amino acids of human milk
s7.aa1: Human milk protein is mainly intact protein, then peptides; free amino acids are a small share but may be among the main contributors to taste. Agostoni et al. (2000) and Chuang et al. (2005) both report far higher free amino acid contents in human milk than in formula. The table lists the 17 free amino acids of the 50 human milk samples in Table 2 of Cui et al. (2026); glutamic acid is the most abundant (704 μmol/L, 49.2%).
s7.aa2: Interpretation: the predictions broadly agree with common knowledge: glutamic and aspartic acid umami; serine, glycine, threonine and alanine sweet; leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine bitter. All these amino acids are in the training data, so this only shows that the tool works within its domain. Threonine (umami 34%) and cystine (umami 31%) exceed the umami threshold although the dataset does not record them as umami: a bias of the model itself.
s7.lim: Limitations: The model ignores concentration, matrix and synergy, and most molecules in the tables are in its training data. It cannot be used for safety assessment.
s8.ala.gb: ≥ 12 mg/100 kJ (≥ 50 mg/100 kcal), no upper limit
s8.dha.gb: optional (Table 4): 3.6 to 9.6 mg/100 kJ; if DHA is added, at least as much ARA, ARA ≤ 19.1 mg/100 kJ
s8.q: Question: Can 1-hepten-3-one be used as a flavoring? What do the rules say about the precursors?
s8.r1: 1-Hepten-3-one (CAS 2918-13-0) was not found under any spelling of its name or its CAS number in the texts of GB 2760-2024 Tables B.2 and B.3 (only 4-hepten-3-one, S1262), the EU Union list (consolidated version of 2026-02-16), or US 21 CFR Parts 172, 182, 184 and 189 and the FDA list “Substances Added to Food” (as of the site's data date). As a control, 1-octen-3-one is found in China (S0219), the EU and the FDA list (FEMA 2677), so the search works. Even without Table B.1, it is not listed in any of the three lists.
s8.r2: Infant formula may not be flavored (GB 2760-2024 Table B.1, see step 5); the precursors fall under the nutrient standards:
s8.r3: GB 10765-2021 also requires a linoleic to α-linolenic acid ratio of 5:1 to 15:1. The GB 10765-2021 values are taken from the English translation published by the Spanish Ministry of Health.
s8.lim: Limitations: The site's regulatory lookup covers only the flavoring lists, not nutrient standards; the latest official texts prevail.
s9.q: Question: Where does the flavor of infant formula differ from human milk, and in which direction should it be improved?
s9.tool: Tool: Dairy flavor improver, “my GC-MS data”. The input is the mean relative content from Table S2 of Cui et al. (FC_CITE), arranged in the tool's CSV format (download: human milk HM (n=303, target), cow-milk-based formula CMF (n=10), plant-oil-based formula POF (n=10)); human milk is the target and each formula type in turn the current sample; thresholds are the author group values (identical, one by one, to those of the 27 key flavor compounds in Table 2 of that paper). That study used the same instrument (8890B) and fibre (DVB/CAR/PDMS) as Cui et al. (2026).
s9.h3a: Human milk ROAV: tool and paper side by side
s9.r1: The paper computes ROAV for each sample and then averages; the tool computes it from the mean contents, so the values differ (the tool fixes the largest at 100) and only the ranks are compared. The main compounds rank the same: the top 6 ((E,E)-2,4-nonadienal, 1-octen-3-one, 1-hepten-3-one, hexanal, (E)-2-nonenal, nonanal) and ranks 11 to 13 are identical. The exceptions are two swapped neighbouring pairs: (E)-2-octenal and octanal (ranks 7 and 8), and (E)-2-decenal and (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal (ranks 9 and 10). The tool finds 3 more compounds with ROAV ≥ 1 than the paper: (E,E)-2,4-decadienal and 2,3-octanedione (both below 1 in the paper) and 1-octen-3-ol (not listed for human milk in the paper).
s9.h3b: Gaps between formula and human milk
s9.fig: Odor profiles of cow-milk-based formula (solid) and human milk (dashed), human milk / formula 12-dimension view.
s9.alt: Radar chart screenshot of CMF against human milk in the dairy flavor improver
s9.r2: Cow-milk-based formula (CMF): 18 compounds compared. Higher contribution share in human milk: (E)-2-nonenal +10.0 (not detected in CMF), 1-octen-3-one +7.0, 1-hepten-3-one +5.4, hexanal +3.6, (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal +2.5 (percentage points, likewise below); higher in CMF: dimethyl trisulfide −9.8 (not detected in human milk), dimethyl disulfide −6.4 (not detected in human milk), (E,E)-2,4-decadienal −5.6, 2-heptanone −5.3 (not detected in human milk), pentanal −3.9, (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal −3.3.
s9.r3: Plant-oil-based formula (POF): 20 compounds compared. Higher in human milk: (E)-2-nonenal +10.0 (not detected in POF), 1-hepten-3-one +5.8, 1-octen-3-one +5.7, (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal +4.7, (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal +2.7; higher in POF: pentanal −7.0, dimethyl trisulfide −6.7 (not detected in human milk), 2-heptanone −5.1 (not detected in human milk), dimethyl disulfide −3.8 (not detected in human milk), (E,E)-2,4-decadienal −2.3.
s9.i1: Interpretation: both formula types differ from human milk in a similar direction: (E)-2-nonenal, 1-hepten-3-one, 1-octen-3-one and (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal contribute more in human milk, in line with the paper's conclusion that human milk aroma is dominated by unsaturated aldehydes and ketones, which showed metallic notes in GC-O; dimethyl disulfide and dimethyl trisulfide are higher in formula, which the paper links to onion- and garlic-like notes, typically formed by Strecker degradation of methionine. For compounds higher in human milk the tool gives directions only, no amounts, and notes that infant formula may not be flavored, so only raw materials, processing and precursors can change; compounds higher in formula have to be lowered through raw materials or processing (for example oxidation control, heat treatment and storage).
s9.i2: Lipid sources (Table S1 of the paper): all 10 CMF contain raw cow's milk; OPO appears in 6 CMF and 5 POF; the lipid sources of POF include no raw cow's milk or cream and are mainly OPO and vegetable oils (soybean, sunflower, coconut, rapeseed, palm and others), 2 of them with added DHA. The paper notes that CMF and POF differ in aroma because their composition differs.
s9.lim: Limitations: The input is the mean of each group, which loses the variation between samples, and each formula group has only 10 samples; ROAV is semi-quantitative, so the two sides are compared by contribution shares, not by value; this step gives directions only, no amounts.
s10.l1.l: semi-quantitative; relies on library identification; reference retention times offset
s10.l2.l: ROAV is relative within a sample; thresholds are for water
s10.l3.l: compounds are in the training data; no cis/trans distinction
s10.l5.l: predicted odor only; infant formula may not be flavored
s10.l6.l: human milk and cow milk data are not comparable
s10.l7.l: ignores concentration and matrix; most molecules in the training data
s10.l8.l: the lookup covers flavoring lists only
s10.l9.l: mean inputs; directions only, no amounts
s10.p1: The chain starts from one raw instrument report and uses 7 tools in turn: data processing (matching the author's program compound by compound) → key flavor compounds (ROAV) → two independent checks against GC-O descriptions and FD → the finding that flavorings are not allowed, which turns the work to precursors → the taste and nutrient rules of the precursors → the gaps and directions between formula and human milk, from the means of 303 human milk samples and 20 formulas. Each tool answers one small question; only together do they lead from a peak table to a formulation.

case.full: One flavor analysis with this site's tools
case.sub: Starting from the original GC-MS report of one human milk sample, the site's 7 online tools are used in turn, all the way to the flavor gaps between infant formula and human milk.
